10.1002_aenm.71171: Cellulose‐based electrolytes are promising solid electrolyte candidates for low‐cost and eco‐friendly batteries owing to their natural characteristics of being renewable and biodegradable. Unfortunately, they have strong reactivity and high crystallinity, leading to critical challenges when used in Li‐ion batteries, including poor high‐voltage tolerance, slow Li‐ion conduction and heterogeneous Li‐ion flux. Here, we report a functional grafting modification to regulate Li‐ion conduction within cellulose‐based solid electrolytes. In‐situ sol‐gel self‐assembly accompanied by amino‐siloxane grafting is developed to achieve the homogeneous integration of cellulose−amino‐siloxane−ionic liquid composites, forming a compact solid‐state electrolyte membrane. Such functional design establishes continuous and uniform Li‐ion transport highways through amino coordination while disrupting native crystallinity of cellulose, endowing a rapid Li‐ion conductivity (1×10 −3 S cm −1 ) and a high electrochemical oxidation potential (5 V). The obtained electrolyte membrane features a homogenous microstructure with high mechanical elasticity and thermodynamic stability, exhibiting high compatibility with Li metal and enabling excellent electrochemical performance. Consequently, solid‐state Li‐metal batteries exhibit exceptional cycle‐life, whereas LiFePO 4 cells run 592 cycles and LiNi 0.8 Co 0.1 Mn 0.1 O 2 cells run 403 cycles at 0.5 C rate until the capacity reduces to 80%. Notably, a comprehensive life‐cycle assessment verifies its advantages in energy conservation and carbon reduction. It presents a sustainable development of high‐performance cellulose‐based solid‐state electrolytes.
10.1016_j.csite.2026.107869: Efficient thermal management is essential for ensuring the safety, reliability, and longevity of Li-ion batteries, yet liquid-cooled plate (LCP) designs face persistent challenges in balancing cooling efficiency with hydraulic performance. This study presents an AI-based integrated workflow for the design and optimization of LCPs featuring leaf-inspired bifurcation geometries. The framework consists of four sequential stages: data analysis, predictive modeling using GMDH-type ANN, Pareto-based optimization via multi-objective arithmetic optimization algorithm (MOAOA) and multi-objective particle swarm optimization (MOPSO), and final design ranking with the WASPAS decision-making method. The GMDH models demonstrated high predictive accuracy, achieving R 2 > 0.99 for thermal resistance and pressure drop. Both MOAOA and MOPSO produced nearly identical Pareto fronts, confirming robustness in capturing trade-offs between thermal and hydraulic performance. Optimized inputs revealed balanced designs at mass flow rates of 0.8–1.5 g/s, channel widths of ∼3.7–3.9 mm, and heights of 2.4–2.5 mm, achieving thermal resistance of 0.25–0.35 K/W with pressure drops of 10–25 Pa, ensuring efficient cooling without excessive hydraulic penalties. Decision analysis revealed context-specific optimal designs, ranging from ultra-low thermal resistance (0.1793 K/W) at the cost of high pressure drop (106.81 Pa) to energy-efficient solutions with minimal pumping penalties (ΔP = 2.14 Pa).
10.1021_acs.jpclett.6c02610: Electrochemical reactions occur near electrode surfaces─this interfacial environment has long obscured the mechanistic insight required to improve selectivity and overall rates. While traditional linear spectroscopies can be used to probe bulk chemical changes, the interfacial response is buried within, limiting insight into solvation environments that modulate homogeneous electrochemical transformations. Here, we address these challenges by studying the protic catalytic mechanism of a Cr-based bipyridine catalyst capable of the selective reduction of carbon dioxide (CO2) to carbon monoxide (CO), at an applied potential using sum frequency generation (SFG) vibrational spectroscopy. Measurements on a series of increasingly complex samples allowed for the characterization of species and solvent environments in an electrochemical solution at a gold working electrode surface. SFG spectra show how applied potential affects the packing of molecules and their conformations at interfaces to allow catalytic species to approach and transfer electrons─emphasizing the divide between species in the bulk versus at the surface and underscoringthe need for further research in this area.
10.1021_acsami.6c15509: Conventional CdS-based photoanodes exhibit limited intrinsic polarization and severe carrier recombination, which hinder the full utilization of piezopolarization electric fields for charge separation in piezo-photoelectrocatalytic (piezo-PEC) water splitting, thus restricting their energy conversion efficiency. In this study, a doping-induced defect-dipole engineering strategy is proposed, in which La-doping leads to in-situ sulfur vacancy formation and thus a VS-Cd0.97La0.03S photoanode was successfully fabricated for piezo-PEC water splitting. The main principle behind this strategy is the construction of oriented La3+-VS dipoles, which are added in-phase with the natural electric field due to piezopolarization. Such a configuration significantly increases the strength of the built-in electric field and its alignment across space, creating highly efficient paths of carrier migration. Benefiting from this synergistic reinforcement, the VS-Cd0.97La0.03S photoanode shows excellent piezo-photoelectrocatalytic activity: it achieves a current density of 3.15 mA cm-2 at 1.23 V vs RHE, which is significantly higher than that of pristine CdS and other published analogues. The results of density functional theory calculations also confirm that the performance enhancement is a result of increased coupling between oriented defect dipoles and piezopolarization fields as well as improved orbital hybridization. Both these effects interact to regulate the built-in electric field and dynamic behavior of carriers. The present study establishes a design framework for the efficient control of carrier separation and transport in multi-field synergistic catalysis.
10.1021_acscatal.6c05801: Iridium-based catalysts remain essential for enabling durable oxygen evolution in proton-exchange membrane water electrolyzers (PEMWEs), yet their surface and subsurface chemistries remain insufficiently resolved by conventional characterization methods. Here, we establish time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (ToF-SIMS), combined with multivariate analysis, as a framework for deconvoluting chemical-, structural-, and depth-dependent features across commercial IrOx powders spanning amorphous and rutile phases. Static and Ar cluster-sputtered ToF-SIMS spectra reveal distinct surface hydroxylation, oxide fragment distributions, and subsurface chemical signatures that differentiate amorphous and rutile IrOx and expose synthesis-dependent residues. Across all powders, surface regions are enriched in hydroxylated IrOx fragments, while subsurface regions show increased reduced Ir species and carbon-based ions. ToF-SIMS fragments are correlated with X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) extracted parameters, providing complementary surface chemical information that supports species identification. Finally, integrating ToF-SIMS and XPS descriptors with electrochemical and structural metrics yields a chemically resolved picture linking hydration depth, oxidation state distribution, and structural order to catalytic behavior. This multi-technique, multivariate framework provides insight into the chemical features governing Ir-based OER performance and supports the rational design of robust, efficient catalysts.
